name: Wadden Sea
blurb: Tidal mudflats where worms, cockles and millions of shorebirds meet.

tip.title: Remove the cockles
tip.text: Cockles feed red knots and oystercatchers and are also eaten by crabs. Cut the common cockle and watch which shorebirds and crabs lose food.

notes: The story and why it matters come from the Wikipedia articles listed below (Wadden Sea, Red knot, Bar-tailed godwit). Individual species and links have not been checked one by one. Feeding links that match a GloBI (Global Biotic Interactions) record are marked in the node details, with a link to the records. A few links were added from GloBI records.

nodes.desc: Drifting algae carried in with the tide. Filter feeders such as cockles and mussels strain them from the water.
Forms dense beds on the flats by attaching to each other and to hard bits of ground. A preferred food of eiders and oystercatchers.
A diving sea duck that swallows mussels whole and crushes them in its gizzard. It also eats crabs and other crustaceans.
An opportunistic gull of the coast that feeds on shore crabs and other items found on the flats.

nodes.name: Harbour seal
nodes.desc: Rests on sandbanks at low tide. Eats mainly fish, including flatfish, and occasionally shrimp and crabs.
Light reaching the exposed flats at low tide lets mud-surface algae and eelgrass grow.
Nitrogen and phosphorus carried in from rivers and the sea. Bacteria in the mud release them again from dead matter.
Twice daily the sea floods and uncovers the flats, setting feeding times for birds, fish and shellfish.

nodes.name: Mud bacteria
nodes.desc: Break down dead algae, plants and animals in the mud and return nutrients to the water.

link_ideas.with: Arctic tundra breeding grounds / West Africa wintering coasts
link_ideas.what: Red knots and bar-tailed godwits breed on Arctic tundra and winter along European and African coasts, using the Wadden Sea as a refuelling stop.
Another major red knot stopover, where birds feed on horseshoe crab eggs.

story: The Wadden Sea is a shallow tidal sea of about 10,000 km² along the Netherlands, Germany and Denmark. At low tide, mud snails and cockles feed on the mud, and red knots eat them. Bar-tailed godwits dig out lugworms.
matters: It is a World Heritage Site and an important stop for migrating birds. Sea level rise is a major threat to its low-lying tidal flats.
